newsitem.title: UK: UK electronic commerce vision unrealistic - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK electronic commerce vision unrealistic - survey.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
British business has overblown expectations for electronic commerce generated over the Internet, a survey showed Wednesday.
According to KPMG Management Consulting, Britain"s top companies expect to generate sales of about 170 billion pounds a year over the Internet in five years.
But unless companies invest seriously, and soon, these hopes are unlikely to materialise.

"This estimate (of 170 billion pounds in British sales) is made despite very low levels of investment in the technology and the fact that more than 80 percent of the companies questioned cannot currently attribute any sales whatsoever to the Net," KPMG said.
The survey reveals very low investment plans in Internet technology, and miniscule current sales generated through the worldwide computer network.
"Things would have to change pretty drastically for this to be achieved," KPMG partner Paul Baker told a news conference. "We are wondering how they are going to do it."

The survey, of 100 British companies with sales exceeding 200 million pounds a year, showed they expected 17 percent, or almost one in five of their sales, to come directly via the Internet in five years time.
This compares with between two and three percent now.

"However, the survey also shows that companies' current and planned levels of investment in the Internet are very low and out of all proportion with their expectations," KPMG said in a statement accompanying the survey.
The companies involved in the survey were from the finance, manufacturing, distribution and retail sectors.

"This gap between sky-high expectations and reality means that companies need to gain more knowledge of the Internet, more investment, and a serious look at how companies can benefit from this," KPMG consultant Jonathan Barling-Twigg said.
The world of electronic commerce generates more hype than fact.

Studies forecasting a world of future consumers lounging at home with their personal computers ordering pizzas, holidays, shopping, insurance or doing their banking, tend to have steeply pointing graphs.
At one end, sales tend to be close to zero. The projection over five years or more often extrapolates sales into the billions.

At a recent conference in Paris, IDG, the U.S. information technology consultancy and publisher, reckoned that by 2000, 27 million European households would own personal computers, up from two million in 1995.

Hewlett-Packard Co executive vice-president Rick Belluzzo talked about "pervasive computing", where information technology would become a utility like electricity. Devices would be as ubiquitous as toasters and electric shavers.
This vision may be well on the way to becoming true in the U.S., where 39 percent of homes have personal computers, compared with 25 percent in Britain and Europe's 20 percent.
But in Britain urgent action is required to kickstart the infomation age into life.
